# Proposal: Deployment of an Internal AI Assistant Across the Organization

## Background

Organizations are increasingly using artificial intelligence to improve employee productivity, accelerate access to information, and support better decision-making. Within our 5,000-employee organization, employees routinely spend significant time searching for policies, locating documents, preparing routine communications, summarizing information, answering recurring questions, and navigating internal systems. These activities create avoidable administrative effort, produce inconsistent answers, and place pressure on specialist teams such as Human Resources, Information Technology, Legal, Finance, and Operations.

This proposal recommends the deployment of a secure, organization-wide internal AI assistant that enables employees to interact with approved organizational knowledge and productivity tools using natural language. The assistant would provide answers grounded in authorized internal content, assist with common workplace tasks, and direct employees to authoritative sources when additional review or action is required.

The proposed solution would operate within the organization’s existing security, identity, privacy, and information-governance frameworks. It would not replace professional judgment, established approval processes, or accountable decision-makers. Instead, it would provide employees with a practical digital support layer that improves access to information while maintaining appropriate controls over confidential data, regulated content, and high-impact decisions.

## Objectives

The primary objective is to make reliable organizational knowledge and routine assistance available to employees through a secure, easy-to-use AI interface. The initiative will pursue five related outcomes.

First, it will improve employee productivity by reducing the time required to find information, draft routine materials, summarize documents, and complete repetitive knowledge-based tasks. Second, it will improve the consistency and accessibility of internal guidance by connecting employees to approved policies, procedures, standards, and frequently used resources. Third, it will reduce demand on service teams by deflecting appropriate routine inquiries while preserving clear escalation paths for complex or sensitive matters. Fourth, it will establish responsible enterprise practices for the use of generative AI, including governance, transparency, data protection, human oversight, and continuous monitoring. Finally, it will create a scalable foundation for future AI-enabled workflows across departments.

## Scope

The initial deployment will serve all employees through the organization’s standard identity and collaboration environment, with access controlled through existing role-based permissions. The assistant will support general workplace use cases such as answering questions about approved internal policies and procedures, locating relevant documents, summarizing provided content, drafting emails and reports, preparing meeting summaries, generating first drafts of routine communications, and guiding employees to the appropriate service channel.

The assistant will initially connect to selected, high-value knowledge sources, including current corporate policies, employee guidance, IT support documentation, operating procedures, approved forms, and selected departmental knowledge bases. Each source will undergo ownership, quality, access, and freshness reviews before being made available to the assistant. Content that is obsolete, duplicated, unowned, or subject to unresolved access restrictions will be excluded until remediation is complete.

The initial scope will not include autonomous decisions affecting employment, compensation, promotion, discipline, eligibility, legal outcomes, financial commitments, safety determinations, or customer or citizen rights. The assistant will not independently send external communications, modify authoritative records, approve transactions, or execute material changes to business systems. Any future expansion into these areas will require separate risk assessment, business ownership, testing, and approval.

The project will include employee training, acceptable-use guidance, support procedures, technical monitoring, security testing, privacy review, and a communications program. It will also establish a formal process for reporting inaccurate, unsafe, biased, or inappropriate responses and for correcting the underlying source content where necessary.

## Proposed Approach

The deployment will use a phased implementation model that balances speed with organizational readiness and risk management. A centralized program team will establish the common platform, security model, governance framework, and technical standards, while business units will nominate priority use cases and content owners.

The assistant will use enterprise authentication and existing access permissions so that employees receive only information they are authorized to access. Responses will be designed to cite or link to source materials wherever feasible, allowing employees to verify information and reducing the risk of unsupported or misleading answers. The experience will clearly communicate that AI-generated responses may require review and that authoritative policies and designated subject-matter experts remain the final source of truth.

Before broad release, the organization will conduct structured testing using representative employee questions, adversarial prompts, sensitive-data scenarios, accessibility checks, and performance tests. Results will be reviewed by Information Security, Privacy, Legal, Records or Information Governance, Human Resources, and relevant business owners. The release decision will be based on documented acceptance criteria rather than technical readiness alone.

## Timeline

The project is expected to take approximately twelve months from authorization to full organizational deployment.

During the first two months, the program will establish executive sponsorship, confirm funding, appoint business and technical owners, complete the initial risk and privacy assessments, select the technology approach, and define the governance model. The team will also identify priority use cases and inventory the internal content sources most suitable for the first release.

Months three and four will focus on solution design and preparation. This phase will establish the identity and access architecture, data-handling standards, logging and monitoring requirements, integration approach, content-cleanup plan, support model, and employee communications strategy. Initial content owners will review and prepare the materials selected for the pilot.

During months five and six, the organization will build and test a pilot environment for approximately 300 to 500 employees representing different functions, roles, technical abilities, and geographic or operational contexts. The pilot will measure usefulness, accuracy, adoption, response quality, security controls, and support demand. Participants will receive training and clear guidance on appropriate use.

Months seven and eight will be used to evaluate the pilot and refine the solution. The project team will address technical defects, improve retrieval and response quality, expand or revise the knowledge base, adjust policies and training, and confirm that support and incident-management processes are operational. A formal go/no-go review will determine whether the organization is ready for a broader launch.

Months nine and ten will support a controlled rollout to approximately 1,500 to 2,000 employees across additional business units. This phase will validate scalability, departmental content ownership, communications, accessibility, and service-desk readiness under substantially higher demand.

Months eleven and twelve will complete the organization-wide deployment to the remaining employees. The final phase will include ongoing monitoring, post-launch evaluation, executive reporting, and a prioritized roadmap for additional integrations and use cases. After launch, the program will transition from project delivery to an operating model with continuous improvement and quarterly governance reviews.

## Resource Requirements

The initiative will require an executive sponsor with authority to resolve cross-functional issues and maintain organizational alignment. A program manager will coordinate delivery, budget, dependencies, communications, and reporting. Product ownership will be provided by a business lead responsible for employee value, prioritization, and adoption.

The core implementation team should include enterprise architecture, AI or machine-learning engineering, application and integration development, identity and access management, cybersecurity, privacy, legal, information governance, data or knowledge management, user experience, accessibility, organizational change, training, procurement, and service-desk representation. Business units will provide subject-matter experts and content owners to validate use cases, approve source material, test responses, and maintain content after launch.

For an organization of this size, the project should plan for approximately 12 to 18 dedicated or substantially allocated full-time equivalent staff during peak implementation, supplemented by part-time representatives from business and control functions. This estimate includes program leadership, product management, technical delivery, security and privacy, content preparation, testing, training, communications, and support readiness. After deployment, a permanent operating team of approximately 6 to 10 full-time equivalent staff, supported by departmental content owners and governance participants, should maintain the service, monitor performance, manage incidents, and coordinate enhancements.

The budget will include platform or licensing costs, implementation services where required, cloud or hosting costs, integration and identity work, security testing, content remediation, employee training, communications, accessibility support, monitoring, and ongoing operations. A contingency reserve should be included to address unexpected integration complexity, data-quality issues, regulatory requirements, or additional security controls. Final budget approval should follow completion of the technology assessment and pilot design, but the organization should treat ongoing operations as a recurring service cost rather than a one-time project expense.

## Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use

The assistant will be governed by a cross-functional steering committee representing executive leadership, Information Technology, Information Security, Privacy, Legal, Human Resources, Information Governance, Communications, and major business functions. The committee will approve the use-case roadmap, establish risk tiers, review performance and incidents, and authorize expansion into higher-risk capabilities.

Every connected knowledge source will have a named business owner responsible for accuracy, permissions, retention, and review frequency. The assistant will respect existing access controls and will maintain appropriate audit logs for administrative activity, system performance, user feedback, and security events. Logs will be handled in accordance with privacy, retention, and employment policies.

Employees will receive clear guidance on what information may be entered, how responses should be validated, when human review is mandatory, and how to report concerns. The assistant will be prohibited from presenting itself as a human decision-maker or from giving definitive advice in areas requiring professional, legal, medical, financial, employment, or safety judgment. High-risk requests will be redirected to designated experts or established processes.

Performance monitoring will include accuracy, source attribution, refusal behavior, privacy compliance, security events, accessibility, user satisfaction, and disparities in performance across relevant user groups. The organization will periodically review whether the assistant is producing unsupported answers, exposing information incorrectly, or encouraging inappropriate reliance. Corrective actions may include updating source content, changing system behavior, restricting a use case, retraining users, or temporarily disabling a capability.

## Success Criteria

The deployment will be considered successful when it delivers measurable employee value without compromising security, privacy, compliance, or trust. Within six months of organization-wide launch, the program should achieve active use by at least 60 percent of employees, with at least 35 percent using the assistant monthly. Adoption targets will be adjusted by role and access to technology so that usage is evaluated fairly across the organization.

At least 70 percent of surveyed users should report that the assistant helps them complete routine information or drafting tasks more quickly, and users should report an average time saving of at least 20 percent for selected priority use cases. For approved knowledge questions, the assistant should achieve a minimum grounded-response rate of 90 percent in structured testing, with source links or citations provided for at least 90 percent of applicable answers. Responses that cannot be supported by approved content should clearly state that limitation rather than speculate.

The program should produce a measurable reduction in avoidable demand for participating service teams, with a target of 15 percent fewer routine inquiries in selected categories after sufficient adoption. At least 80 percent of pilot and post-launch users should indicate that the assistant is easy to use, and accessibility testing should confirm that the service meets applicable organizational and legal standards.

No material security or privacy incident attributable to the assistant should occur. All critical findings identified during pre-launch testing must be resolved or formally accepted by the appropriate risk owner before wider release. The organization should also maintain documented ownership for 100 percent of connected knowledge sources and meet defined review intervals for all high-priority content.

Finally, success will be measured not only by usage but by sustained trust and responsible operation. The assistant must have an active governance process, transparent employee guidance, reliable support and escalation channels, regular quality reviews, and a funded roadmap for improvement. If the service meets these criteria, it will provide the organization with a secure and scalable foundation for improving productivity while establishing the controls necessary for broader, responsible adoption of artificial intelligence.

Employees will authenticate using their current credentials, and access to information will be governed by existing permissions wherever technically feasible. At the conclusion of the rollout, the project will transition to a permanent service-management model with scheduled performance reviews, content-owner responsibilities, security monitoring, and a prioritized roadmap for future enhancements.

In pilot and post-launch evaluations, the organization should achieve a measurable reduction in time spent locating information and completing selected drafting, summarization, and preparation tasks.

The organization will review these measures quarterly and use the results to determine whether to expand integrations, introduce workflow automation, or revise governance controls.

## Conclusion

Deploying an internal AI assistant across the 5,000-employee organization represents a practical opportunity to improve productivity, strengthen access to institutional knowledge, and establish responsible enterprise capabilities in artificial intelligence. A phased implementation will allow the organization to demonstrate value while managing technical, operational, privacy, and adoption risks. With strong governance, reliable content, appropriate human oversight, and sustained investment in training and support, the assistant can become a trusted digital service that helps employees work more effectively while preserving the organization’s standards for security, accountability, and quality.
